Description: A business firm is a needs-satisfying machine; it is an entity invented and employed by society to better satisfy society’s interests[1]. ‘Value’ is created when the customer is willing to pay (such) a price for a product/ service/ combination thereof that exceeds the costs incurred to deliver the same. Value creation occurs across the ‘Supply Chain.’ For a given ‘Value,’ the supply chain evolves to minimize the sum of the input, conversion, and transaction costs. This course introduces the vocabulary, perspectives, concepts, and models used to study and analyze supply chains.

Course Rationale :
This course helps students understand Organization, Organizational Theory, Structure, and Design. It
also introduces some of the key concepts like Change Management, Decision-making, Culture,
Conflict, Power, and Politics. The primary purpose is to enhance the student’s knowledge of how the
structure, systems, and selected issues influence organizational processes and performance. Students
will be able to relate how managers and organizations can build organizational culture, implement
planned change, and how conflict, power, and politics are integral aspects of the organizational
system.
Course Objectives :
CO1. To develop critical thinking on important theoretical themes in organizational theory and
evaluate the organization's dynamic process based on the same.
CO2. To develop abilities to assess and describe organization showing linkages between environment,
strategy, and structure and point out solutions.
CO3. To acquaint the participants with some of the key organizational issues like decision-making,
culture, knowledge management, conflict, power, and politics.
Learning Outcomes :
LO1. Will be able to critically comment on the usefulness and practical implication of the theoretical
underpinnings of organizational theory.
LO2. Will be able to apply fundamental concepts of organization theory and structure to understand and
solve organizational dilemma.
LO3. Will be able to evaluate the role of strategy, structure, and decision making process in organization.

Course Description:
The course aims to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of portfolio management
principles, including constructing and evaluating investment portfolios.
Topics we cover include the market indices, efficiency frontier, the Markowitz portfolio, capital asset
pricing, model, arbitrage pricing theory, factor models, active and passive investing, smart beta, beta
core, bucket investment, simulation, optimization, Sharpe ratio, Traynor ratio, Mutual funds etc.
Course Objectives:
The course objectives are as follows:
1. Gain knowledge of financial markets
2. Understand risk and return dynamics.
3. Develop an understanding of portfolio management
4. Develop skills in investment strategy
5. Enhance decision-making abilities
Learning Outcomes:
1. Understanding risk, randomness, and market efficiency
2. Understand mutual funds
3. Constructing an optimal portfolio
4. Evaluating the performance of a portfolio
Remarks: Approved by CC, Course Code awaited

Description:
Course Description:
Today's world is borderless; everyone is accessible to anyone and anywhere in the world. This happened because of the advancements in technology and innovation, which businesses are constantly working on. This is one side of the story, and the other is that there are threats to society, such as inequality, hunger, poverty, climate change, wars, etc.  To overcome the problems, governments, businesses, non-governmental organizations, and other stakeholders are working significantly to improve people's lives and economic growth and development. They need finance to overcome and cope with the emerging challenges essential to achieving the 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The SDGs are important and cover almost all life, business, and developmental aspects of the environment and industry.

This course explores the possibilities and issues with the impact of finance on achieving Sustainable Development Goals and the relationship between them. As finance is essential for achieving SDGs, here comes the role of a manager, one who manages businesses. With their actions in the industry, managers will try to accomplish these without delays. Which is benefit the society at large. Hence, managers need to understand the different aspects of SDGs and how they finance them with the available funds.

This course introduces different financial instruments to achieve world-level SDGs and gives a case study of the Indian story. 


Learning Objectives: 

Students will be able to understand the fundamentals of SDGs. 
Students will understand the emergence and development of the SDGs.
To understand the role of finance in achieving SDGs. 
To examine the financial instruments for SDGs.
To learn about different issues and difficulties in achieving the SDGs.


Learning Outcomes: 
Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:
Understand the importance of SDGs.
Gain skills and knowledge on the finance and SDGs nexus
Understand the importance of financial instruments in achieving the SDGs.
Develop an SDGs index to compare the different countries/states.
Critically understand the role of Government, NGOs, and other stakeholders in achieving SDGs
Remarks: Approved by CC, Course Code awaited

Description:
Economists primarily use mathematical methods to make and study economic arguments. Mathematics brings in the rigour and precision that are required to ensure that the economists’ statements are true and logically sound. This course is intended to familiarize students with mathematical concepts and methods typically used by economists, and introduce ideas from topics in differential and integral calculus, optimization, linear algebra, and financial economics. A course in these topics will lay the foundation for more rigorous courses in (various branches of) economic theory, statistics and econometrics.

The goal of the course is not to delve into the theorem-proof route, but rather to help the students develop their mathematical reasoning and intuition, and become comfortable talking about economics using mathematical shorthand.
Remarks:
Preference given to 2nd year students. 
Open to students in years 2, 3, and 4

Description:
This course has a dual focus: First, to introduce you to probability theory and the basic statistical concepts that are used to explore and understand economic phenomena. Second, to show you how this statistical knowledge can be applied to real world data using widely available spreadsheet tools like Microsoft Excel. Therefore, this course has been designed very much from a practitioner’s point of view. You will find that the material that you learn in this course will have direct application in your jobs and further studies. Sound grasp of material from this course will also be essential for your further coursework in econometrics and advanced microeconomics.

The topics covered in this course fall into three broad categories: descriptive statistics, probability & distributions, and hypothesis testing. Descriptive statistics deals with the visualization and summarization of statistical data. You will learn simple tools for visualizing data on one and two variables, as well as statistical concepts for summarizing the central location and dispersion of your data. In the probability & distributions section, you will learn about probability and surrounding concepts like sample spaces, random variables, and combinatorics. You will also learn about some common discrete and continuous probability distributions. Hypothesis testing deals with questions of statistical inference: when are our conditions supported by the data and when are they not? You will learn about samples, and populations, point and interval estimates, and the apparatus of hypothesis testing about one or two variables.
Remarks:
Preference given to 2nd year students. 
Open to students in years 2, 3, and 4

This course is aimed at introducing economics students to statistical programming, using R and Stata. In this course, students will learn the basics of programming – such as downloading and installing the programme(s), managing libraries and packages, and good coding practices. Students will learn to perform simple computations, including basic mathematical operations, creating vectors and variables, and working with frequently used tools such as conditionals and loops. 

Through a combination of lectures, hands-on exercises, and projects, students will be exposed to different data structures, and learn the tools to manipulate and analyse data – importing data from different sources/in various formats, and transforming them into a format suitable for analysis, cleaning data and dealing with missing information, and data visualization/description – creating and formatting charts and tables. Based on students’ comfort level with these foundational skills, the course may also touch upon additional topics related to simple statistical tests and analyses.

Description: This course is a sequel to Microeconomics II specially designed for the students enrolled in the FYUP. It will focus on the study of market failure under second best settings. It will also dwell deeper into game theory, public goods, factor markets, and time costs. The concept of the market equilibrium will be re-introduced, and we will learn how the characteristics of the market vary in the real word leading to conditions such that market fails to achieve an equilibrium, focusing on externalities, public goods, markets with asymmetric information and imperfect competition. The course would develop a rigorous set of tools to analyze such conditions while unraveling how choices can interact and persist leading to strategic outcomes and payoffs.

Description:
This course is an immersive exploration of the complex relationship between our environment and economic systems. We will tackle pressing environmental challenges, diving into diverse perspectives on both environmental issues and economic analysis. You will encounter both established and cutting-edge approaches, equipping you to critically evaluate solutions.
Beyond economic theory and environmental policy frameworks, we will delve into real-world case studies, sharpening your ability to apply learned concepts. Prepare to engage with international environmental issues, global sustainability concerns, and the economic development equation. We will even explore the philosophical underpinnings of environmental thought.
This course emphasizes practical policy tools, empowering you to analyze and potentially shape solutions for a sustainable future.
Remarks: Open to students in years 3 and 4.

Description:
The course is about public-sector economics from historical, theoretical and policy perspectives. While the theory explains the rationale for the existence of why the state plays a distinct role in market or capitalistic economies, social and fiscal policies
explains how revenue (i.e., taxation) is collected and spending (e.g., social insurance, welfare, etc..,) is made by the union-state-local governments and their impact in the economy in the historical perspectives of developing countries like India and the developed world. This will help to reveal the changing conceptualization and praxis of theories and policies over time. Specifically, the course focuses on three major topics:
●	Historical & economic rationale for the public-sector
●	Social insurance & redistribution 
●	Theory & practice of taxation
Remarks: Open to students in years 3 and 4.

Description: Labor economics, in a comprehensive sense, involves examining how individuals, firms, institutions, and the public sector interact to influence employment and wage outcomes. Throughout this course, we will delve into both theoretical and empirical aspects of labor economics, placing a significant emphasis on practical applications. We will focus on discussing research designs aimed at empirically measuring theoretical predictions and assessing the impact of policy interventions.
Remarks: Open to students in years 3 and 4.

Description: The economy, which we have come to think of as a distinct sphere of human activity, is a peculiar conceptual construct with an even more peculiar history. This course introduces economics majors to influential intellectual traditions that continue to shape how we think about the economy and the laws that govern it. Along the way, the class will revisit and historicize commonplace categories in the field of economics: commodity, money, capital, prices, wages, rents, etc.
Remarks:

Open to students in years 3 and 4.

Description:
Since the early days of Adam Smith and David Ricardo, economics as a discipline has been interested in the principles and policies surrounding international trade among nations. As the economic integration of nations has intensified over the past five centuries, culminating in the most recent era of globalization since the 1990s, International Economics has assumed greater significance and relevance for students of the discipline of economics.
 
This course will cover the history and origin of International economics and trade. The course aims to acquaint the students with the theoretical underpinnings of trade and introduce them to trade instruments and the policies adopted by trading nations. It will focus on the constitutes of international trade and the theories that explain why trade takes place in the first place. It will introduce the students to the currency of trade and the rates at which it is exchanged: floating, fixed, spot, forward, expected, pegged, managed, and trade-weighted, to the economics behind factors that drive exchange rates. The course will discuss issues related to imports and exports, current and capital account balances, national savings identity, and the global flow of capital. As trade protection instruments, tariffs, quotas, subsidies, dumping, CVDs, etc., will be learned. 
 
Relevant historicity will be provided; for example, the Smoot Hawley Tariff will be discussed, and its role in the economic depression of 1929 will be investigated. Students will be introduced to Mercantilism, the Gold Standard and the Bretton Woods System, the concept of the Reserve Currency, the 1970s oil shocks, and the factors that led to the transition of the GATT to the WTO. The course will introduce the students to the changing world order of increasing share of services in trade, the Free Trade Agreements, and the QUAD.
 
The course funnels into a deeper study of international economics and finance.
Remarks: Open to students in years 3 and 4.

Course Title: World History from 1750 to the present( Formerly known as: HIST209 : How We Became Modern: World History from 1750 to the Present)
Description: We take the idea of being modern for granted. Yet historians have long debated what it means tolive in a modern world. Did modernity emerge in Europe and spread around the world over thelast five hundred years? Are all parts of the world equally modern? Has the idea of what it meansto be modern, modernity, been used to justify radical and (often) violent actions by various 20thcentury governments? In this course we will try to answer these and several other questionsusing rich scholarship produced by the field of global history from the discovery of the NewWorld in the 15th century to the globalized world of the present. Among other things we willstudy about the enlightenment, the emergence and fall of European empires, the integration ofthe global economy and the environmental fallout of globalization.
Remarks: Previously the course title was How We Became Modern: World History from 1750 to the Present

Course Title: From Mughaliyah Saltanat to Sovereign Republic: India in Transition
Description: This course will study the processes that transformed India from a Mughal Empire to aSovereign Republic. Until 1857 the Mughal emperor remained the fount of political legitimacyof South Asia even as the actual power of the Mughals waned. Mughal successor states includingAwadh, Hyderabad, Bengal and even the British East India Company at least nominally drewtheir authority from the Mughal crown. By 1950 India had emerged as a republic whose rulersderived legitimacy from democratic elections. India’s evolution from Mughal empire to colonyto independent republic raises many questions. How did social, economic and political forcesradically transform South Asia in under a century? What effect did colonialism have on India?How are the lives of ordinary Indians today different from those of their ancestors living twocenturies ago? Themes covered in this course will include colonialism, nationalism,decolonisation, social reform movements and state formation in the South Asian context

To eat, like breathing, is a biological instinct of our bodies, necessary for daily functioning. Unlike breathing however, the ways in which we eat, the food items we choose or reject, are linked to societal norms and economic capacities, beyond individual agency. This course will read foodways as systems of communications that encode identities in terms of state and household institutions, geographical markers, religious affiliations, labour and class positions, and caste and gender norms.

This course will move chronologically through the turn to agriculture, ancient states and empires, religious sacrifices and asceticism, medieval mercantilism, industrialisation and circulation of food and labour, and end in the present day post-globalisation world. We will learn to read primary sources ranging from the pots and pans of the ancient world, medicinal texts, religious canonical literature, oral and written recipe collections, and modern day popular culture. Together, we will use these contexts and sources to understand how food functions as a marker of identity.

Course Title: Themes in Economic history: Humans as Planetary Pilots
Description:
This course intends to explain economic events and phenomena in their historical contexts,
recognizing such thinking to be central to the discipline of economics itself, from Adam Smith
to Thomas Piketty. Economic history seeks to explain fundamental questions about wealth and
inequality in relation to both individuals and nations. Such historicizing will help us understand
(a) how technologies, institutions, and innovations will spur economic growth and (b) how the
wealth generated thus is redistributed. This course has two core objectives: first, to present a
general introduction to economic history by examining how labour, technology, and commerce
have remade human cultures since the Neolithic Revolution; second, to explore specific topics
in relation to modern economies since the Industrial Revolution. Taught by economists and
historians, the specific topics chosen may change.

Course Title: Power and Powerlessness: Caste, Class and Gender in Indian History
Description: This interdisciplinary course explores the dynamics of power and powerlessness in society with a specific focus on class, caste, and gender. Through critical analysis, discussions, and case studies, students will examine the interplay of social structures, inequalities, and systems of privilege and oppression. The course aims to empower students to become informed and active advocates for social justice.

Course Title: Pre-Socratics and the Socratics - History of Philosophy
Description: This course will introduce students to thinkers who collectively formed the philosophical tradition of the ancient Greece. It will first familiarize students to the philosophical thoughts of the pre-Socratic thinkers like Thales, Pythagoras, Parmenides, Heraclitus and Democritus. Then, the focus of the course will shift to Socrates, and the two major Socratic philosophers – Plato and Aristotle. Students will be introduced to the ethical and metaphysical concerns of these three thinkers through the selected works of Plato and Aristotle. Philosophical themes including moral virtues (like justice, wisdom, piety etc.), good, beauty, happiness, death, God and soul will be explored in theses classes. Taking a historical approach, the course will enable students to systematically and critically reflect on specific philosophical issues that were relevant to the ancient Greeks.

Course Title: Theorising Technology (Formerly: PHIL335 - Introduction to Philosophy of Technology)
Description: Human evolution is tied to the question of technological evolution, or perhaps vice versa. In either scenario, questions of – what is technology? How does technological design structure the world around us? What are the requirements of adapting to the demands of technological change? What are the larger socio-political and ethical implications of technological change? All these questions need to be situated as part of a discussion in the philosophy of technology. The course seeks to introduce the students to some of the seminal thinkers and their positions in this respect and engage them in fundamental ontological queries regarding technology.

This is an introductory course to the classical Indian philosophy of language. The title has been taken from Bimal Krishna Matilal’s monograph from which we will be reading some portions. In this course, we will be walking through four schools of Indian philosophy – Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, Buddhism and Grammar – to understand various theories of word (śabda), meaning (artha), sentence (vākya), powers of the word (śabda-śakti) and how to derive meaning from them. Along the way, we will be discussing questions such as, how many meanings can a word denote? Does language simply denote the world that we live in,
represents it or creates and shapes it? Who decides the meaning – the speaker, the listener or the language in which it is communicated?
We will also touch upon some deeper philosophical questions like, does language reveal the truth or veils it? Can there be a soteriological function related to language? Through the
classical texts incorporated in the course, the students will gain beginning competence in reading primary texts through translations. The aim is to encourage the students not only to
learn the Indian theories and philosophy of language but to think with them – critically, comparatively and creatively.

Course Title: Philosophical Concepts: Objects and Subjects I : Intro to Metaphysics
Description: In this introductory course, we will engage with basic questions in metaphysics - one of the foundational pillars of philosophy. Questions such as what is reality? What is the nature of truth? How do we experience and know about things around us? Have been central to philosophical enquiry. We will explore these questions by foregrounding the concepts of objecthood and subjecthood. We will examine whether these two seemingly different concepts are related and what this understanding implies for philosophy. The question of objects is a central to understanding ontology and its role in experience. What defines objects? Are objects created or discovered?  What kinds of objects are there? We will study the various conceptions of objectivity including explorations of realist, idealist, modal theories on objects and so on. Similarly, the question of subjects is central to the epistemological enterprise. There are many ways of thinking about the subject. How has the subject been understood via materiality, reason, substance, language, society, interests? What is intersubjectivity? This course primarily explores metaphysical questions concerning objectivity, subjectivity, experience and the knower and their implications across disciplines, be it science, mathematics, arts or the social sciences.

Description: This course explores the evolution of Indian politics from Independence to the present-day BJP-led government.

Course Title: Politics in Multiple Frames: Approaches, concepts and theoretical perspectives
Required for: Required Course for Politics Major / Minor, Politics-History Joint Major
Description: This course seeks to outline various perspectives of understanding politics at multiple levels from the local to the national to the global. Is politics essentially about power, government and elections, or is it about friends and foes? Could it be about a deep yet contested conversation about public goods or an art of bringing political differences into an integral but tension-ridden whole? Students will develop a foundational understanding of historical, empirical and normative dimensions of politics at each of these scales. What are the pressing questions that we encounter at different levels of politics, and how did the systems that organise them come to be, and what are the epistemologies and power dynamics that underpin them? How does the academic discipline of politics constitute its objects of study and protocols of enquiry? Can the focus of politics be exclusively on human action, and such a focus be sustained in times of deep ecological crises?

Required for: The study of politics is much more than the study of the state. It involves the examination and engagement with the social and political structures, concepts, ideas and values. Thus, concepts like equality, liberty, rights, justice, sovereignty, power, democracy, modernity, nationalism, identity, state, legitimacy and dissent become central to the discipline of politics. Political Theory I exposes the students to some of these concepts. However, the course on Political Theory II will engage with the remaining concepts through the ongoing debates around some of the concepts like sovereignty, power, nationalism, democracy, identity and modernity. The engagement with these debates bring to the surface how certain concepts complicate or simplify the understanding and applicability of other concepts in a polity. The engagement with these concepts manifests in political action. Political action aims at either preservation or change guided by the thought of better or worse. This is deeply embedded in finding the good or the right driven by what starts as a question and ends with knowledge. Thus, political theory is driven towards the pursuit of knowledge for the good of society, polity, people and collectives exhibited in the establishment of order and resolution of contestation or conflict. The engagements with ongoing debates enhances this pursuit of knowledge which is deeply embedded in explanatory wisdom for the truth. Thus, the course will engage with such a quest for knowledge while resolving ongoing contestations, conflicts and debates that aim at generating consent and acceptance for an ordered polity. The course will be anchored to the challenges to state and sovereignty, contestations over power and legitimacy, debate around dissent safeguarding democracy or democracy being dissent, paradox of modernity and identity and the elusiveness of nationalism. It is through a critical engagement and coherent analysis of the concepts and the ongoing debates and challenges around them that the course will enrich political theory and the discipline of politics as it will create the knowledge of the whole by putting the parts together.

Required for: The socio-cultural construction of the body is intrinsic to the constitution of the self. The body does not just define the ‘self’ but also the ‘other’ or ‘non-self’. The body is a source of knowledge while understanding social positioning and is understood through everyday living. Beauty is closely connected to the body. It is defined in terms of the perfect body and bodily appearances. In fact societies have been obsessed with a beautiful body for long. The body is a strong communicator and has a specific political anatomy of its own. It can see and is also constantly seen by the others. The course will look at the body from a political perspective and navigate through questions like what constitutes the body and how we see them. It will help in understanding the process of othering that constantly takes place in the socio-economic-political-cultural milieu we inhabit. By taking the body as the source of intervention, the course will engage with questions of self, identity, subjectivity and objectification. Thus, engaging with the sociological construction of the body, politics of visibility or that of seeing and be seen, heightened presence of technology, bodies as embodiment of caste, religion, space and disability becomes unavoidable and pivotal. It opens up the domain of alternative narratives that make us look at the body as made up of a plurality and multiplicity of bodies. The course will draw from articulations and conversations that have already been initiated by scholars like Judith Butler, Michel Foucault, Erving Goffman, Bryan Turner etc to enrich the discourse on body politics.

Description:
This course is designed as an analytical, contextualised introduction to Indian foreign policy and
 strategic thinking. The course is designed to enable students to follow contemporary debates in
 an informed and critical way, and from multiple points of view. Traditionally, this topic is taught
 through a historical approach and an overview of bilateral relationships. This course will merge
 that with elements from foreign policy analysis courses, that is, by including themes such as the
 influence of domestic politics and non-political issues. It will begin with a contextualising
 historical overview and then briefly examine contributing factors that shape thinking and policy
 on India’s external relations before looking specifically at key relationships and important policy
 areas.

In broad continuity with the course Introduction to Comparative Politics, this course involves a deeper engagement with the key themes and methodological approaches that constitute the dynamic field of Comparative Politics. This course offers an advanced exploration of conceptual variables such as state formation and state capacity, social movements, and civil society as well as ideologically conditioned political processes such as democratisation, and development across supra-national, national, and local levels. The thematic composition of this course is informed by gender and intersectional lenses. Beginning with the evolution of the field beyond its Euro-American moorings, the course will delve into the diverse methods that characterise comparative research. This is followed by a historically contextualised study of dominant political ideologies. Other key themes covered in the course include political parties, representative democracy, and contemporary phenomena such as populism.

Course Title: Social and Political Thought: Intimations of Modernity
Required for: Required course for the Politics & Elective for Social Studies, Philosophy Major/Minor
Description: This course deals with ideas articulated by individual thinkers such as Machiavelli, Hobbes, Locke, Mill, Weber and Marx on society, politics, and power. In addition, it covers different ways of thinking of ‘past’, their attendant imaginaries, and the politics of identity and recognition in the modern world. Both these parts are connected by and anchored in the stories of ‘modernity’. ‘Modernity’ is a large and complex theme that encompasses transformations in the sphere of economy, politics, society and morals. It does not offer a unitary story. We also know that it has become a global currency for justifying as well as critiquing power. Separated by a long stretch of time, how do we make sense of these ideas? How these thinkers, spanning a period of four centuries, were not only shaped by significant sociopolitical changes but also created new ways of comprehending them? The course brings interpretive and methodological resources from sociological theories, political philosophy, and historical imagination to examine ideas and experiences that define ‘modern’ life and their embattled presence in our time.

Course Title: Citizenship, Exclusion and Belonging in South Asia ( CC Approval awaited)
Description: This course explores historical and contemporary perspectives on citizenship in South Asia, examining how colonial legacies, postcolonial state-building, and competing nationalisms have shaped mobility, rights, and exclusion. It analyzes the role of religion, caste, gender, and ethnicity in defining belonging, with particular attention to the experiences of marginalized communities such as Dalits, Adivasis, religious minorities, and refugees. The course also addresses how citizenship intersects with social and economic inequality, and engages with contemporary issues including partition legacies, documentary citizenship, climate displacement, and rising ethno-nationalism.

Course Title: Ethnography of Political Violence (Formerly: SOCL215|PSYC222 - Anthropology of Violence: State, Power, and Politics)
Required for: Elective course for Social Studies Major / Minor
Description:
This course explores violence in both its everyday, normalized forms and its spectacular, visible eruptions. We will examine how violence is unequally distributed, disproportionately impacting women, Dalits, Adivasis, Muslims, and queer communities—whether through lynching, sexual violence, riots, or incarceration. Often premeditated rather than spontaneous, violence gains legitimacy through imagined injuries to caste, gender, or national order, and is frequently sanctioned by society, with perpetrators enjoying impunity.
 
 We will also study “extraordinary” forms of violence—war, militarization, genocide—and critically reflect on how anthropologists study violence, including the ethical and methodological challenges this entails. Through ethnographic case studies, with a focus on India and neighboring regions, we will explore how violence is intertwined with democracy, how political and social orders define what counts as violence, and how certain lives and actions are rendered punishable—or invisible.
 At its best, work in this field exemplifies the power of rigorous, reflective scholarship under conditions of strain, disrupting what is taken as normal or natural in the social order. At its worst, however, it risks devolving into voyeuristic representation—amplifying trauma without adequate critique or care, and at times, inadvertently perpetuating the very dynamics it seeks to examine. This course offers a critical engagement with the phenomenology of political violence, with a particular focus on recent anthropological literature that explores these tensions and possibilities.
Remarks: Approved  (Previously the course title was Anthropology of Violence: State, Power, and Politics and previous course code was SOCL215|POLT222)

Description:
In the 20th century, the entire world came to be divided into "underdeveloped", "developing" and "developed" countries. Underlying this division was a hegemonic project of "development", an extended process of structural transformation associated with industrialization and modernization of economies and societies. Since the 1960s, this consensus has unravelled in several ways. First, there have been many normative critiques of development understood as industrialization and modernization, as well as many alternative normative agendas for development (e.g. human development, inclusive development, sustainable development). Second, both in popular and academic discourse, there has been a reconsideration of the respective roles played by governments, firms, non-governmental actors, social movements, etc. in the development process. As a result, the political economy of development has emerged as a field of enquiry rife with debates between scholars and practitioners of markedly different theoretical persuasions and political beliefs.
 
 This course will encourage students to simultaneously engage with development debates at three levels: a) theoretical antecedents; b) policy paradigms; and c) specific policy interventions in the Indian context. Each theoretical tradition has been matched with an important policy paradigm and a policy controversy emanating therefrom. The list of debates includes: balanced vs. unbalanced growth, import substitution vs. export promotion, liberalization vs. industrial policy, growth vs. basic needs, energy transitions vs. degrowth, and alternatives to capitalist development.

Course Title: Law, Society, Abolitionism (previously: SOCL336 - Sociology of Law)
Description: This course offers a theoretical understanding of law, and prisons in society, as well as the concept of abolitionism. Students will read recent first-person accounts of surviving prisons in India.

Course Title: Ecofeminist movements in India (Formerly: SOCL325|ENVS325 - Eco feminism)
Description: The course views environmental movements in India as a grassroots social and political initiative that adheres to Gandhian tradition of nonviolence and aimed at ensuring the survival and livelihood of working-class individuals, as well as indigenous and tribal communities. These movements, shaped by indigenous socialist, spiritual, and ecological principles, seek to empower marginalized communities in their decision-making regarding natural resources while reinforcing the essence of inclusive democracy. The course particularly observes the role of women in these movements who remain at the center of resistance or participated in the collective actions in a noticeable way. In addition to uncovering lesser-known instances of women's social resistance against environmental injustices (e.g. resistance against monoculture), the course will emphasize prominent ecofeminist movements in India, such as the Chipko movement, Narmada movement, and the Western Ghats movement. Taking an interdisciplinary approach, the course encompasses feminist theories, literature, including theater, art, dance, poetry, and fiction that altogether represents a local ecofeminist discourse of knowledge and power regarding women, environment, and society.

Required for: Elective in Global Arts (3 and 4 year Minor-can count as Practicum requirement (Arts immersion) Concentration in Global Arts, Litt-Arts Major
Prerequisites to enrol for this course: The course is built for practitioners of music, dance, theatre and any other form of performative art practice. Learners will be expected to learn the gestures and abhinaya and perform them in a seated position. This practicum course is meant to immerse up and coming artiste practitioners in the specialized art of Baithak Bhav and enhance skills for narrative performances in any form.
Description:
Abhinaya or the art of emoting using gestures and facial expressions including subtle shifts in body language, glances, gaits etc, to evoke a response/ reaction in the spectator by invoking the theme’s (poem’s) innate disposition. This is a practice-based course for dancers and musicians of all genres, theatre practitioners, movement artistes and those with a flair to learn performance, to unpack in great detail and nuance the poetic intent using interpretive methods, predominantly through the art of Abhinaya (Bhav). Using the torso, upper body, the limbs and gestures for abhinaya in a seated position, Baithak Bhav is one of the most ancient and challenging improvisational skills taught as part of various performative traditions. In learning this form of narrative building and story- telling, students will work with chosen poems across multiple languages including Telugu, Sanskrit, Tamil and Urdu, while reflecting on ideas of subtexts, stable and transitory emotions and psychophysical responses. The central questions this practicum focuses on are, how can the performer/actor intensify the innate nature of a theme’s substratum to create high magnification of response in the viewer? How can they use their own core nature of personality and ability to sustain the paradigmatic emotion of śrngārā- passion? Course Objectives/ Learning Outcomes
 
 To gain foundational knowledge on performing Baithak Bhav using expressions and gestures including to sing the poetry that is being performed.
 Learning to read multi-lingual poetry through text and translation.
 Learning to place the poem in context, using historical, social and psychophysical analysis of characters and nature.
 To engage in thought provoking discussions on thematic substratum and ways of representations in narration as well as to intuitively respond to poetry through abhinaya.

Course Title: The heard, seen and felt- Indian Canons and Intellectual traditions on theories of Aesthetics and Processes of Production
Required for: Elective course for Global Arts minor (3 and 4 years), Litt- Arts Major, concentration in Global Arts, Psychology Elective, Philosophy Elective
Description:
Understanding the complex codes of performative production involves studying the connection between word and meaning, movement and play, the processes involved in the manifestation of Rasa (aesthetic pleasure), thinking about its ontology- whether it comes from the writer, character, actor or the audience? How can emotions be conveyed without being told, and how the expression of quotidian life obscures spatio-temporal constraints of the mind to experience the joy of consciousness. Concepts like these become central to this course. In close-reading texts on Indian aesthetics and drama and following the arguments by logicians over centuries, we investigate how passion (Rasa) is foregrounded as a particular aspect of the ego which, when intensified through performance is “tasted” by a responsive audience. Read in texts and translation from Sanskritic, Tamil and vernacular works, the class will engage in debates over foundational theories from Indian intellectual traditions and also draw comparative ideas from European aestheticians such as Kant, Barthes and others. Between writing, seminar and debate sessions, the course will help the student investigate and include themselves within the discourse on aesthetic judgement and its impact on social and moral judgements in new medias and the real world.
 
 
 
 Course Objectives / Learning Outcome
 
 The student will learn critical concepts from Indian intellectual traditions on performance
 Will learn to engage in healthy debating, an age old intellectual tradition called Tarka, as a pedagogical method in this course
 Will enhance the thinking and processes of production for writers, actors, dancers, musicians and all other forms of performance and creative practitioners, including new media creators like photographers/ mixed media creators, technological, scientific, psychological and social thinkers.
Remarks: 1. Reading knowledge of Sanskrit or Tamil is not mandatory for this course. Alhough the course will work with extant texts, concepts will be dealt with in translation. 2. Students are encouraged to take the course Baithak Bhav-Techniques of Improvisation and Composition which is being offered in this trimester, as an added advantage to practically better understand some of the modes of production discussed in this class. But, this is not mandatory.

Course Title: Modern-day Storytelling - an introduction to documentary filmmaking and its use in peoples’ and environmental movements
Required for: Elective for Global Arts (3 and 4 years Minor), Litt-Arts Major, Concentration in Global Arts, Environmental Science Elective, History Elective
Description:
Documentary films are modern, technology driven storytelling. A
 medium that can turn anyone’s life and its stories into interesting visual
 narrations. This course follows the journey of the camera from being a
 tool that exudes aesthetics, creativity, and capturing of memories, to
 becoming the strongest instrument of resistance in the struggles of
 ordinary people. Through a series of interactive lectures the students
 will explore how the medium of documentary filmmaking can bring
 stories that are invisibilized, to light. 
 The course will bring parallel experience of learning the history,
 evolution and basic use of camera, the most critical tool in
 documentary filmmaking, along with understanding its use in capturing,
 propelling and archiving peoples’ movements in India. In the 12 weeks,
 students will practically explore the camera and use it to capture life
 around them and create a short documentary. The course will also
 cover basics of all other skills such as sound recording, scripting,
 storyboard development, logging, transcription and editing involved in
 producing a documentary film. This course will take them through
 important steps such as learning of method, ideation of concept,
 shooting and post-production of a documentaryfilm.
 At the core of documentary filmmaking lies the critical concept of
 integrity, the ability to visually capture stories of people and the world
 just as we see it. Hence, this course will allow students to not only
 immerse themselves in historicity, but also develop ethics in practice.

Required for: Elective in Global Arts (3 and 4 year Minor-can count as Practicum requirement (Arts immersion) Concentration in Global Arts, Litt-Arts Major
Prerequisites to enrol for this course: Students with prior experience with clay and ceramic processes, or those who have taken a pottery/ceramics course, would be given preference.
Description:
Firing is an integral and very important step in ceramics, as it is what makes the clay durable because it puts the clay through an irreversible chemical change, so it no longer slakes in water. After this, the fired clay can be broken into smaller and smaller pieces, but they will not disintegrate nor degrade. 
 This step of firing, although ancient, is not just a simple act of putting the clay in flames. The way that clay is fired has developed and evolved across time and geography, and continues to change, depending on the function of the ware being fired, the resources available, limitations, and the desired aesthetic and utilitarian outcome. 
 This course studies this process, the aids to firing, as well as the variety of ways to use the process as part of the creativity. It’s the science of the art.

Required for: Elective in Global Arts (3 and 4 year Minor-can count as Practicum requirement (Arts immersion) Concentration in Global Arts, Litt-Arts Major
Description:
Students get a glimpse of the variety and chemical composition of clays, as well as insights into the continuous historical context of using it as a material in craft, art, and science through the ages. The creation of small to large functional as well as sculptural ceramics, (working as individuals as well as collaborative work in pairs, or groups), will be the bulk of the hands-on studio work. 
 Students will also learn ways of decorating the clay surface at different stages; when wet, when leather hard, and when bone dry. They will learn how to use techniques of altering, adding/subtracting of clay, (including making pieces with the kuruniki techniques), then using coloured slips and engobes, (coloured using metal oxide additions), they will learn inlaying, (mishima), engraving, sgraffito, brush work, slip trailing, pouring, dipping, etc. 
 They will simultaneously study techniques and ware produced by traditional communities around the world as well as contemporary artists and studio potters who specialize in particular techniques. Time and budget permitting, there may be short field trips. Some selected pieces made by them will be fired, and there will be an opportunity to showcase and display the pieces produced by them, to the larger Krea Community. 
 The course is a combination of lectures, talks, demonstrations, slide shows, films, a lot of hands-on work, regular practice sessions for skill development, readings, discussions, and the possibility of a field visit, time, logistics, and budget permitting.

Required for: Required for Litt majors, minors, concentrations
Description: The Introduction to Creative Writing is an intensive writing workshop designed to give students the opportunity to develop their craft via in-class workshops, readings, discussions, and one-on-one tutorials. The discussions will also focus on publishing and the publishing industry. The course will include Zoom sessions with authors and literary agents. The class will mimic the frenzied pace of real-life publishing. There will be deadlines, drafts, and redrafts. We will learn to read like writers and write like writers under pressure. Students will turn in one fully realized piece of fiction (a short story or the first chapter of a novel in progress) and a book review for the course. For the book review, students will choose a work of fiction by an author who comes from a background different from theirs (we will discuss in class what this means) on which to write a paper and give a presentation. The paper will be divided into two sections – the first will be a 1,000-word review of the book, and the second will be an analysis of the reviews the book has garnered in the media. The analysis should include students’ thoughts on the audience the book was written for, the type of marketing that might have gone into the book, the cover, the hooks used to gain publicity, author interviews, etc. You will need to search The New York Times, New Yorker, Guardian, Washington Post, Hindustan Times, Hindu, Financial Times, and other publications for reviews and features on the book. You will give a 10-minute presentation on your review.
Remarks: To be capped at 15: preference to be given to declared Litt majors and minors

Course Title: Brief Encounters: The Short Story Through Histories and Cultures
Required for: Elective for Litt majors, minors, concentrations
Description: If brevity is indeed the soul of wit, then the short story is the fictional equivalent of modernity: it captures the burst of a moment, a shifting mood, a passing shadow. In fact, in some ways the short story is the arch-genre of modernity. In the early to mid-19th century, the modern metropolis was being forged by capital, migration and anonymity; here rapid industrialisation made demands on uninterrupted time; the telegraph and the railways atomised distance; photography made possible the visualising of an instant. It is in that kind of a city where print modernity took sharp turns and the short story became one of the founding genres to mirror the harried, hurried, fleeting life in the new metropolis. It came to belong to a space in between a sketch and a tale, a fable and a saga, an anecdote and a long narrative. This course would look at the cultural and social origins of the short story; enquire into the ways in which it has transformed over the last century and a half; look at some of the critical approaches to it; and study its astonishing fecundity and flourish in the Indian subcontinent, much of which embraced the genre rather early. In short, this course will be both a survey of the genre as well as one which would look closely at some of its most representative specimens, and in languages (translated) as varied as Russian, English, Spanish, French, Urdu and Bengali.

Required for: Elective for Litt majors, minors, concentrations
Description: The course revisits the idea of humour as an artistic, cultural and humane practice and powerful, potential and often radical form of critique across nations, genres, tongues and political climate. The course intentionally mixes up canonical and comparatively unknown texts so that students are able to respond to them both in terms of their own power, as well as their location in cultures from which they emerged.

Course Title: Ancient Greek Drama and its Modern Adaptation
Required for: Elective for Litt majors, minors, concentrations
Description: Written to be staged in the annual festivals of fifth-century Athens, the plays of classical Greece rank among the finest and most enduring works of western literature. The tragedies of Aeschylus or Sophocles, and the comedies of Aristophanes, have inspired artists, writers, and philosophers over twenty-plus centuries. What is it about the plays that has caused them to be so widely studied and adapted through the ages?—all the love, lust, murder, and revenge? their mythology? or their inquiry into psychology and morality? More fundamentally, what is it about their form and structure—their innovations in the media and modes of poetry and performance—that makes them so effective in expressing concerns of such vital and perennial interest, and so amenable to adaptation and translation? We shall consider these and other questions by examining, closely and carefully, both the plays themselves as well as their adaptations in art, literature, and film.

Course Title: The Uses of Orthodoxy - the Poetry, Criticism, & Cultural Theory of T. S. Eliot
Required for: Elective for Litt majors, minors, concentrations
Description: Of all the poets and critics of high modernism, it is perhaps T. S. Eliot who stands least in need of an introduction: his poems form the mainstay of literature curricula from high school through university; his essays and criticism continue to inform our understanding of art, literature, and culture; and the scholarship surrounding his work, enough to fill a library, is not for the faint of heart. And yet, there is one aspect to Eliot that is usually glossed over, namely, his thoroughgoing commitment to orthodoxy. Introducing a collection of his own essays in 1928, he described their “general point of view” in words that apply to his works as a whole: they are, he said, “classicist in literature, royalist in politics, and Anglo-Catholic in religion.” Clearly, then, Eliot saw no real contradiction between his commitment to orthodoxy on the one hand and his radical socio-cultural critique and literary innovation on the other. He saw them, rather, as being in concert, the former a condition for the latter, and the latter as a means of building and broadening the former. This relationship between conservatism, critique, and creativity will be the vantage point from which we shall take a comprehensive survey of Eliot’s works. The course will be divided into three modules. In the first, we shall outline Eliot’s definition of tradition, as something, not fixed or ossified, but ever growing and ever evolving, not as a hindrance to creativity, but a necessary condition for it. We shall begin with some intellectual history, by tracing similar conceptions of tradition in Matthew Arnold, G. K. Chesterton, and W. B. Yeats before coming to some of Eliot’s more celebrated essays: “Tradition and Individual Talent,” “What is a Classic?,” “The Function of Criticism,” along with shorter pieces on individual writers. In the second module, we shall see this conception play out in Eliot’s own major poems. We shall read poems that reflect his deep dissatisfaction with the broad tendencies of modern life, from spiritual and philosophical to sociological and cultural. And from these poems we shall draw out Eliot’s defence of tradition, negatively at first, but also more and more positively. We shall read them intertextually: we shall attend closely to how Eliot positions them in literary history; how he sets them in conversation with great poems of the past; and how doing so allows for the sort of originality, in both form and meaning, that helps remedy the anxieties of modernity. Finally, in the last module, we shall dwell upon the one aspect of Eliot’s thought that is most often overlooked, namely, his religious convictions. We shall consider the ways in which Eliot’s understanding of religion, as the fundamental category of life and thought, informs his poetry as well as his understanding of culture and society. To this end, we shall conclude with two of his most important works on religion and culture, Murder in the Cathedral and Notes towards the Definition of Culture.
Remarks: New course: CC approval pending: Capped at 20

Required for: Elective for Litt majors, minors, concentrations
Description: Advanced Creative Writing is a twelve-week course in which students expand on the skills they acquired in Introduction to Creative Writing. You will master the elements of fiction via workshops, one-on-one tutorials and multiple rewrites. You will wax eloquent about plot and dialogue (did someone groan at “action beats”?). You will talk craft and lyricism and resolution. You will finesse your voice and form. You will birth compelling characters in well-thought-out settings. You will continue learning the rules of writing and break them with aplomb. This is a painfully intensive course. Be prepared for double the reading and writing you did in Introduction to Creative Writing. At the end of the term you will produce two fully realized short stories, which, the professor realizes, is difficult to accomplish in three months. You, the student, need to realize this, too, and embrace the chaos of real-life publishing. There will be innumerable drafts, redrafts and deadlines. Each draft you produce will be up for your peers’ consumption. You will all work as editors to help make a story the best it can be. Zoom meetings with practitioners of fiction, editors and agents will further your understanding of the publishing world.
Remarks: New course: CC approval pending; to be capped at 15

Required for: Required for Biological Sciences Major and Minor
Prerequisites to enrol for this course: Scientific Reasoning (SCR), Data Analytics (DAN), Mathematical Reasoning (MR)
Description: Based upon selected case studies, this course covers notions of scale from building blocks of life to biomes, organisational levels and integration of biological units, and the primacy of description. We start with Aristotelian classification and proceed through Early Modern natural philosophy and natural history to the discipline of biology itself in the present day. We consider the development of particular philosophies and forms of technology from the 17th to 19th centuries and corresponding development of elements of biology at different points in time, including such concepts as biogeography, ecology, evolution, cell biology, genetics, anatomy, and physiology, even as theological holds over the subject begin to waver.
Is this course prerequisites for any fut: BIOS224 (Evolution), BIOS218 (Biochemistry), BIOS221 (Genetics), BIOS222 (Plant Diversity and Reproduction), BIOS241 (Ecology and Conservation Biology), BIOS232 (Methods and Communication), BIOS235 (Animal Behaviour), BIOS401 (Plant Anatomy and Physiology), BIOS307 (Comparative Genomics of Bacteria)

Required for: Required for the Biological Sciences Major and Minor
Prerequisites to enrol for this course: Life at Different Scales (BIOS201), Scientific Reasoning (SCR), Data Analytics (DAN)
Description: How did life first arise on Planet Earth 4 billion years ago? In this course, which comprises both organismal and molecular evolution, we will begin with early theories of evolution that lead up to Darwin and Wallace's theory of natural selection. We thus gain insight into the process of scientific inquiry that resulted in one of the most important theories in the biological sciences, before concluding by integrating it with Mendel's theory of genetics referred to as the Evolutionary Synthesis. The course will look at the evidence of macro and micro evolutionary processes, and the evolution of plants and animals to understand the basis of the diversity of living organisms on Earth. Through numerous examples, students will learn about adaptive strategies at the level of individual organisms that may underlie evolutionary changes at the level of a population. At a molecular level, we trace the evolution of life, starting from self-replicating molecules, to the RNA world, to the evolution of cellular components. Along the way we will discuss the role played by the constituent molecules of life. We will discuss the origin of the field of molecular genetics from the Evolutionary Synthesis, bringing the disparate fields of evolutionary biology and genetics together. We will discuss the development and employment of the molecular clock and the salience of neutral mutations in establishing relatedness among organisms, using such markers as mitochondrial, chloroplast, ribosomal and nuclear genetic material, aided considerably by such technological advancements as protein electrophoresis, leading to the amplification of DNA using the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for whole genome sequencing. This course will briefly discuss how the sequence information comes together with the current computational power to draw the phylogenetic tree of life.

Required for: Required for the Biological Sciences Major and Minor (starting with the 2022-26 FYUP batch)
Description: CMB is an introduction to the principles that guide the multifarious processes in the cell at the molecular and cellular levels and is intended for a college level audience. The content is an answer to the question: What is the molecular basis of cellular structure and function? Concepts covered include the storage, transfer, and regulation of genetic information, the interactions between molecules, and their assembly and disassembly in cellular functions, the cytoskeleton and its role in cell and tissue shape, molecular traffic between the various cellular locations and across the membrane boundary, signaling within the cell and between cells, cellular metabolism, the cell-cycle, division, growth, development, differentiation and death, and the energy conversions that power all these processes. The course will focus more on principles than on encyclopedic detail, and will be linked to modules taught in earlier trimesters to enable comprehension.

Required for: Elective for Biological Sciences Major and Minor
Prerequisites to enrol for this course: Life at Different Scales (BIOS201); Evolution (BIOS224 can be taken as a co-requisite)
Description: This course will begin with an overview of animal behaviour and how it has integrated concepts from many disciplines to advance the field. Next, animal behaviour will be studied from an evolutionary perspective before understanding the bases for the variation in behaviours within and among individuals, populations, and species. With these concepts in mind, a range of behaviours will be examined using case studies. Finally, more complex behaviours related to social interactions among animals will be considered.
Remarks: Enrollment will be capped at 24 students, with preference given to graduating BIOS majors

Required for: Elective for Biological Sciences Major and Minor
Description: The course begins with introducing the plant’s meristem and its histological organization to the students, followed by the anatomy of the leaf and other simple & complex tissue structures and their organization. Water is important to plant life, and other mechanical phenomena happening inside plants, such as diffusion, osmosis, plasmolysis, imbibition, guttation, transpiration, etc., are considered. It introduces the stomata & the mechanism of opening & closing that enable gas exchange between plants and the atmosphere. Identifying the essentiality of nutrients is foregrounded, along with their roles, the mechanism of uptake of nutrients, and the mechanism of food transport within plants. What role does gravity play, and how will plants grow in space?  We learn about concepts of photosynthesis and pigment systems/photosystems. Other important phenomena are discussed, such as photophosphorylation, the Calvin cycle and photorespiration in plants. Carbon fixation, indoor and otherwise. How pollution affects them etc. We consider how and why plants go under nitrogen metabolism, how molecular nitrogen fixation happens, and its significance to the world. Plants also need/use hormones for their growth and development. We discuss how growth hormones such as auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid, and ethylene work. We complete the circle by looking at the seed. We introduce students to seed dormancy, its germination, and the concept of photoperiodism and vernalization. We talk about genetically modified plants and seeds (GMOs) and the hazards and ethical issues around them. The genetic basis of the adaptations in plants and how they vary with the types of climates, for example, how do they become resilient to drought? A brief introduction to modern plant biotechnology and gardening is also discussed. Concept integration and awareness about ecosystems, global warming, forests and the plantation of trees

Course Title: Ways of Knowing: Instrumentation in Biology
Required for: Required for Biological Sciences Major for the 2022-25 batch, Elective for Biological Sciences in the FYUP; Elective for Chemistry Major
Prerequisites to enrol for this course: At the discretion of the instructor
Description: In this offering, one of a two-part course, we will discuss the tools available to biologists to investigate the biological systems. We will cover the principles of optics behind the ubiquitous microscopes from 1620 to the recently developed super-resolution microscopes, which culminated in 3 Nobel prizes in 2014. We will explore other types of microscopes, such as the fluorescence microscope, electron microscope (transmission electron and scanning electron), scanning probe microscope, and atomic force microscope. We will also discuss the development of molecular probes, for example quantum dots and fluorescent proteins, and their application in biology. This course will elaborate the use of X-ray and neutron crystallography to determine the molecular structures of the DNA double helix and protein molecules extending to large molecular machines such as ribosomes. The principles of spectroscopy and single-molecule spectroscopy will be explained. We will cover the principle of mass spectrometry and its application in high-throughput biology. We will conclude the course with Nuclear Magnetic Resonance and its application to investigate the structure and function of biomolecules, tissues, organs and cognition.

Required for: Elective for Biological Sciences Major and Minor
Prerequisites to enrol for this course: Life at Different Scales, Genetics or at the instructor’s discretion.
Description: Bacteria are the most dominant forms of cellular life on earth. Their ability to adapt to the entire gamut of environments on our planet is coded somehow in their DNA. We will discuss how this fascinating kingdom of life adapts to its circumstances by studying the structure, organisation and evolution of their genomes. We will take a conceptual and computational approach towards these aims. A particular goal of this course will be to help students conceptualise, design and implement (at least in part) a mini-project analysing bacterial genomes.

This course will enable prospective chemistry majors to acquire the necessary foundation in chemistry to help them to prepare for the later courses in the chemistry curriculum. Electronic structure and periodic properties (3 hrs) Bohr Model, Electronic structure of atoms, periodic table and periodic variations of properties such as ionization potential, electron affinity, electronegativity across periods and groups. Chemical Bonding and Molecular Geometry (3 hrs). Ionic and covalent bonding, Lewis structures, Molecular structure-VSEPR, Molecular orbital theory, hybridization. Gases (2 hrs). Ideal Gas law, non-ideality and van der Waals equation. Kinetic theory of gases, Concepts of pressure, mean free path, collision frequency, Maxwell distribution of velocity and speeds. Basics of Chemical Thermodynamics: (3 hrs) Laws of thermodynamics, Exothermic and endothermic reactions, concepts of entropy, spontaneity, free energy. Fundamentals of Chemical Equilibrium: (3 hrs). Chemical Equilibria, Equilibrium constants, Le Chatlier Brown principle. Acid Base Equilibria: (2 hrs) Bronsted-Lowry theory, Lewis theory, pH and pOH, weak and strong acids, buffers. Organic Chemistry: (3 hrs). Isomerism, stereochemistry, nomenclature, organic molecules of industrial and biological importance, polymers. Reactions: (3 hrs) Oxidation, reduction, substitution and elimination reactions, rates and catalysis. Light matter interaction: (2 hrs) Absorption, emission, scattering, photochemistry.
This introduces physics concepts that will be required for a deeper understanding of chemical and biological systems from a microscopic perspective.
Provide students with a comprehensive understanding of the fundamental principles and concepts governing the behavior of chemical systems concerning energy transformation.

This course builds on CHEM215 and offers more advanced topics in thermodynamics and kinetics. Topics include  chemical kinetics, enzyme catalysis, ionic and phase equilibria, solid state and surface chemistry

It will then proceed to an axiomatic construction of the natural numbers, and introduce the fundamental mathematical notions of sets, relations, and functions. The remainder of the course will be organized around three distinct modules: number theory, permutations and counting, and graph theory.
