Course Title: Software Design Practical (Formerly know as Group Design Practical)
Description: This is a project based course that works towards students having built a complete application of their choosing from ground up, with guidance from instructors. Students will be introduced to programming methodologies and tools and processes (iterative approaches) that will help them with the task. They will also be introduced to the required architectural components and how they interface with each other. The human side of building such applications includes requirements gathering, basic user study, ethics issues and broadly “responsible engineering”.

The course focuses on exploring different operating system design and its functional aspects. The
role of the operating system as a resource manager is detailed with respect to Process
management, Memory management, File management, and Device management. The course also
highlights the operating system and underlying machine communication. Additionally, the course
states the importance of various topics taught in the course in relation to the real-world systems.
Some topics are implemented in program form to have related practical insights.

Formal logic has played a key role in development of modern computer science, with
applications ranging from architecture, databases, verification to AI and theory of computation.
This course will introduce students to proofs and techniques of soundness, completeness and
provability in the formal systems. Formal systems introduced in the course include (but are not
restricted to) propositional and predicate calculus. It will additionally include some of the
resolution theorems from proof theory, which are essential to understand automated theorem
provers

This course will provide an introduction to the foundations of machine learning along with a slew of popular machine learning techniques, which will provide a broad overview of different machine learning tools
follow up course to COMP308

Prerequisites to enrol for this course: Python for Data Science (Required) and Intro to data science (recommended)
Description: This course introduces the students to the field of data science and the kind of problems that can be solved by data science. Students will learn key data science skills, techniques, and concepts, including data analysis, statistical modelling, and some insight into some standard AI/ML algorithms. The course would also bring the perspectives of data from multiple branches of social sciences and provide a fundamental understanding of how data is conceptualized through the prism of humanities and social sciences. Further, the course will cover how data science skills can be used to address some of the vital problems in the field of social sciences. This would be done by a series of guest lectures by faculty members from social sciences. This is a hands-on course where after a quick primer on Python, the student will start with sourcing, processing, and cleaning a dataset. Then, use Python to mine data from its source and analyse available data by using NumPy and Pandas. Subsequently, the student will be introduced to modelling data to perform predictions using the SciPy, scikit-learn, and stats models libraries. In addition, the student will be introduced to visualization methods using the matplotlib and seaborn library to visually understand the patterns in the data. By the end of this course, students will be able to work on data science tasks practically with different Python libraries and achieve their goals.

This course will cover the following topics that are fundamental to the field of data science: Discrete Mathematics: logic, sets, functions, relations, mathematical induction, counting, recursion, trees, and graphs.Probability: axioms of probability; conditional probability and independence; random variables; continuous random variables and limit theorems.
Remarks: Applied Linear Algebra, Applied Statistics, Intro to Statistical Learning, Machine Learning

Prerequisites to enrol for this course: Data Structures and Algorithms and Python for Data Science
Description: This course focuses on database system concepts and architectures, various data models, Database Design using ER models, UML, Relational Algebra etc. Database as well as web-based programming using SQL, PHP etc., will be covered. It also introduces theoretical concepts on database design and normalization, data storage with the corresponding file structures based on indexing using B-Trees, B+-Trees etc. Further, transaction processing and concurrency control principles will be introduced. Some applications on Information Retrieval and Data Warehousing will be covered.

Prerequisites to enrol for this course: Python for Data Science (Required) and Intro to data science (recommended)
Description: Recent advances in computing and information technologies, including hardware, software, databases, networks and communications have enabled the commercialization of many applications of Artificial Intelligence. Specifically, in the case of Supervised Learning, Deep Neural Networks and related algorithms have been able to achieve or even surpass human-like accuracy in applications like face recognition, voice recognition, automated driving, language translation, etc. This has given rise to multiple deployments of AI-based applications not only in the private sector but also in the Government. These deployments in areas such as recidivism prediction, algorithmic online ad targeting, drug addiction risk prediction, criminal intentionality detection in early stage shoplifting, etc. promise the effectiveness and efficiency of evidence-based decision-making. This early success has spurred rapid and frantic development of solutions using AI/ML and associated technologies without adequate safeguards and regulations. However, of late, multiple cases of bias and unfairness have been reported in the decisions made by AI/ML based algorithms, thus, raising ethical questions. In addition, AI/ML-based decisions cannot be explained easily due to their “black-box” nature. Impenetrability of AI/ML algorithmic decisions has reduced “trust” in the very algorithms that promised so much. This has spurred a call for Explainable AI (XAI) – AI-based decision-making that incorporates the notions of fairness, accountability and transparency.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is all around us. It‘s how Google answers our searches, Amazon recommends products, ChatGPT helps answer questions, and Spotify plays another song. Artificial Intelligence is changing the way decisions are being made in the world today. This course is intended to enable students to understand a critical aspect of AI, i.e., industry applications, scenarios, and use cases. The course covers this very critical aspect of AI, i.e., use cases of AI in a variety of industries such as Sales and Marketing, Retail Manufacturing, Healthcare, Education, to name a few.

This course will provide the basic vocabulary that students require to navigate the environmental sciences, humanities, and social sciences. Through systematic close readings of influential texts, we hope to enable students to use the tools and methods employed by these disciplines in the context of the environmental studies. We begin the course by charting out primary motivators and drivers of work in each discipline. We will then home in on cutting-edge research within each discipline. For example, in the environmental sciences, we will focus on the concept of thresholds and safe operating spaces for humanity. During our engagement with the environmental humanities, we will focus on how progress in the digital humanities has enabled visualisation and textual analysis of environmental history, philosophy, ethics, literary theory, art, and education. Lastly, in the environmental social sciences, we will pinpoint how ethnography and narratives are now becoming invaluable tools for understanding how society interacts with the environment.

Environmental studies encompass not only the science of climate change or environmental harm but also communicating these for various kinds of publics. This course moves away from objective and expert accounts of environmental risk and policy to focus on popular and public-facing forms of environmental communication. 
 
Students will read and analyse genres of Environmental Communication like science and nature writing and the photo essay. This course is writing-intensive and the focus will be producing various kinds of
short written and visual pieces and forms of public outreach around case studies drawn from neighbouring ecosystems. As far as possible we will arrange student interaction with some practitioners of these forms.

Environmental science is the study of patterns and processes in the natural world and their modification by human activity. To understand current environmental problems, we need to consider physical, chemical and biological processes that are often the basis of those problems. This course will give you the skills necessary to address the environmental issues we are facing today by examining scientific principles and the application of those principles to natural systems. This course will survey some of the many environmental science topics at an introductory level, ultimately considering the sustainability of human activities on the planet.

Course Title: Environment versus Development: the policy dilemma
Description:
The growth versus environment debate has been one of India’s nay the global community’s major policy dilemmas for over a century now, exacerbated in the era of global warming and climate change. Further deepening the dilemma are the processes set off by globalization, privatization and liberalization combined with the role of technology in people’s lives.
Yet, this debate has also spurred a new line of thinking and public policies in recent times.
Growth is an imperative for material needs or poverty alleviation. But ecology, too, needs to be healthy, in the absence of which there’s a heavy price to be paid by the humanity, as witnessed in the unprecedented disasters: landslides, recurring floods and droughts, water scarcity or the devastation caused by extreme weather events and the society’s unpreparedness in such cases.
It’s a quintessential “wicked problem” – to borrow from the term coined first in a 1973 paper by Horst W J Rittel and Melvin M Webber, professors of design and urban planning at the University of California at Berkeley (Dilemmas in a general theory of planning) – that does not allow for the best solution but rather only the acceptable compromises.
Questions abound: Is there such thing called sustainable economic growth, as advocated by the different stakeholders? What’s the history and philosophy of environmentalism and the many different tensions centred around these two ideas? How does public policy factor in both?
This course, drawing from field work and theoretical foundations, would offer students of social and environmental sciences with a keen interest in public policy a thorough review of this classical dilemma and the choices a society has and makes. 
From the earliest debates over the construction of large dams, to industrial development, to the ideas of green economy or degrowth, and the history of India’s environmental legislation, the week-by-week sessions would build on the different thematic aspects of this debate and pose before students the confounding questions integral to understanding a public policy dilemma.
For instance, the social and economic fallout of the land acquisition for development projects by the State using the whip of Eminent Domain: What happens to the people who are displaced by development projects? This itself posits several questions for consideration: Is development possible without any environmental, ecological or social harm? Or is there a need for a paradigm shift to strike a balance between the two processes, as the world runs out of time to deal with and eventually fix the global poly-crisis, a term coined by historian Adam Toonze.
With class-rooms discussions intermittent with lectures, presentations and anecdotal stories from the field, this course will dwell upon the theoretical foundations as well as the real-life situations to explore tensions between the cause of environmental conservation and preservation and an inevitability of development for economic growth.

Between 1997 and 2020, close to 400,000 farmers have committed suicide in India; nearly 2000 farmers are quitting agriculture every day since 1991, going by the census data 1991-2011, and hundreds of thousands of peasants moving to cities in search of elusive work and livelihoods.
This course will examine the prevailing agrarian crisis in India, its social, economic, cultural and political impacts on the society, particularly the rural. Government responses and media’s role.
Agrarian crisis, typified by a continuing trend of farmers’ suicides, migrations, displacement, high indebtedness, falling incomes, and a general sense of despondency in the countryside, is akin to a Civilizational Crisis (P Sainath, 2019). 
Government and non-government studies have reflected upon the economic, ecological, social, political and other dimensions of this ongoing crisis. 
Engaging students in a seminar-pattern on empirical roots of agrarian problem in India, course will dwell on the continuing crisis of income and sustainability in farming; environmental and ecological dimensions in climate change era; fragmentation of land; problems of equity and access; gender issues; labour; mechanisation; livestock and food systems; credit and finance; post-liberalisation trends in the sector; the fallout of crisis in different states, particularly in the dry land regions; different aspects and faces of this crisis; the responses of the state and central governments and civil society organisations to the problem; the political economy of agriculture; and some models of collectives that are successfully demonstrating a way out.
The course will introduce the aspects of crisis and its fallouts in a way that would help students understand the problems and challenges, and opportunities it throws up in its wake.

Natural disasters are among the greatest threats for human lives and quality of life. This course introduces students to almost all the natural hazards that can cause disasters, from well-known frequently occurring ones to extremely rare ones. The course discusses the causes and consequences of natural hazards, efforts undertaken to predict them in advance and the complications of such efforts, in a fundamental level. The causes of natural disasters are understood based on the underlying scientific investigations. To predict them, routine measurement networks and scientific modelling are required. Finally, mitigating their effect depends on the support and efforts provided by the policy makers.

Materials have shaped history and our everyday lives. The social, political, and economic
structures determining access to materials create varying environmental outcomes.
Environment outcomes in turn shape societies and its practices over time via the
provisioning of materials. Our current thinking about sustainability, conservation, and
environmental crises are all largely shaped by the ramifications of our material relationships.
While philosophers have expounded on the dialectic tensions between the material and the
ideal as an intrinsic feature of the human condition for a long time now, only relatively
recently have the implications of this dialectic tension been explored by scholars of the
environmental studies to better understand environmental and social concerns, both of the
present-day (overproduction, consumer culture, social-ecological fallout), and leading into
the future (New Materialism).
This course is designed to be a whirlwind tour of the various ways to think about
environmental and social contexts underpinning various kinds of materialisms. Past and
present cautionary tales of humanity’s precarious relationship with the material world the
bedrock upon which the dialectic of the material and the ideal hinges on have culminated
in ecological collapse and social strife. However, political, historical, and economic contexts
complicate these simplistic cautionary tales to a large extent with regards to causality. Lastly,
materials are what nourishes our body and our mind, and brings joy to our lives; we delight
in the textures, noises, colours, and tastes of things. Discussions on future materialisms
could be much less likely about how we value material things too much, but rather about
how we don’t value them enough (Thorpe 2014).

The language of ring theory and field theory helps describe fundamental relationships between algebra, number theory and geometry and geometry, and provides a unifying framework for describing certain types of number systems and operator spaces.The course will begin with a study of important families of rings such as Euclidean domains, Principal Ideal Domains, and Unique Factorisation Domains. Course Title: Classical Physics: Energy and Force I
Required for: All Physics major, minor and concentration
Description: Dynamics is the study of the response of objects to applied forces.  Motion has been a subject of philosophical investigations since the time of Aristotle.  It took a very long time before its foundations were laid during the 18th century.  In the process, the subject of calculus was formulated as the then existing mathematical framework was inadequate to succinctly express the empirical observations.   Newton, who finally formalized the required notions to describe dynamics, encoded the known observations in three laws that bear his name.   Two major themes that underlie the conceptual framework of dynamics are force and energy.   Later developments proved Newton’s laws to be inaccurate at high speeds and small distances.   How approximate are they?   Landing on Mars at any specified location still relies on the predictions made using these laws.   For many of our endeavours in science and engineering, these laws are fantastically accurate.   An understanding of dynamics is essential to pursue any of the specialized topics in physics.   Classical dynamics is possibly the beginning of both physics and mathematical analysis. Nevertheless, it continues to inspire new ideas in both subjects.

One cannot imagine the modern world without the impact of electrical and electronic devices. This course will start with a discussion of the basics of electrical circuits, both static and transient. The main course content is centered around the theory of electronic devices based on semiconductors, such as P-N junction diodes and transistors. A study of these basic devices and their applications gives us the necessary background to design advanced circuits. Finally, the course will introduce the basics of digital electronics, covering Boolean algebra and logic gates.

Prerequisites to enrol for this course: Mathematical Methods I, Classical Physics: Energy & Force I (recommended)
Description:
Physics describes nature using particles and waves as basic entities. Newton's laws
of motion govern the dynamics of particles. Sound, ripples on water, etc. are
undulations of the medium in which they propagate. These waves arise due to
interactions among the particles of the medium. Equations governing them are
derivable from the laws of dynamics of particles. But electromagnetic waves do not
require a medium for their propagation. Despite such fundamental differences,
these waves are describable by the same mathematical structure. Physics students
need a good grasp of these ideas since the concept of waves appears in many
contexts such as the wavefunctions in quantum theory, the phonon modes in
condensed matter, etc. This course presents the relevant physics and the
mathematical details required to understand the subject.

The properties of electric and magnetic fields in material media allow us to understand polarization and magnetization of materials. These have tremendous applications in the form of microwaves and electromagnets, and are useful in explaining various chemical phenomena. On the theoretical side, the work of Faraday, Maxwell and others laid the foundation for the first major ‘unification’ of forces in the history of physics – the modern theory of electromagnetism. The behaviour of electromagnetic radiation (light) emerges naturally from this theory, giving us the laws of classical optics. The fundamental incompatibility of electromagnetic theory with Newton’s mechanics was what led Einstein to his special theory of relativity.

Light, being the medium of most observations and measurements, is our window to the physical universe. In this course, we study geometrical optics, where light is described by rays. This deals with basic components like lenses, mirrors and prisms, from which instruments like telescopes and microscopes are built.  In addition, we study the wave properties of light at an introductory level. It includes phenomena such as light interference that accounts for the colours on soap bubbles and has applications ranging from quantum studies to gravitational wave detection. We will also study polarization, which is of importance in photography. In addition, we will discuss diffraction, which is used extensively to study the crystal structure of solids.

Newtonian mechanics is deterministic and applies to a system
with many degrees of freedom. However, propagating a typical initial condition of the
many-body system as per the Newtonian dynamical laws is fraught with difficulties,
both conceptual and analytical. Luckily, if we are interested in a class of macroscopic
properties which correspond to a myriad of microscopic states of the system, one can
profitably employ the language of probabilities. Statistical physics of systems
thermodynamic equilibrium is such a description. A major success of statistical physics
is it provides a dynamical origin to the laws of thermodynamics, though for a restricted
class of systems called ergodic systems. The theory, nevertheless, is applicable to all
systems, microscopic and macroscopic systems included. This course is an introduction
to some of the research questions in statistical physics. Specifically, the course deals
with order theorems, critical phenomena and scaling theory.

Description: Every student of physics, irrespective of whether they wish to pursue theoretical physics or experimental physics, needs a thorough training in the core principles and conceptual structure of physics. The exposure should bring out the coherence and structure in the theories that shape our understanding of nature at all length and time scales. This course is an advanced overview of the discipline that teaches the language of physics as it is practised at advanced levels. This course will enrich and enable students so that they see experiments not as data generating endeavour but as the only way to uncover the deeper principles that seem to be at work in nature.

Prerequisites to enrol for this course: Quantum physics I, mathematical physics I
Description: Physics is an empirical science. Its conceptual framework is revised to accommodate new empirical evidence from experiments. One of the earliest indications for the need to relook at classical physics was the blackbody emission spectrum. The experimental results were at variance with the prediction of classical physics. Max Planck proposed quantized exchanges of energy between the walls of the blackbody and the radiation within. This resolved the discrepancy between the theoretical predictions and the experimental observations. Einstein proposed quantized energy for the radiation field to explain the photoelectric effect. Bohr proposed non-radiating orbits for electrons to account for the stability of atoms and quantized angular momentum to explain their emissions spectra. All these ad hoc procedures found natural explanations in the quantum theory formulated by Heisenberg and Schrodinger. Their ideas were refined and put on firm scientific footing by Dirac, Pauli, Born, von Neumann, Jordan and others.

There is plenty of room at the bottom” is a succinct expression by Feynman about the richness of the quantum world. How do we harness this abundance? In this course, we attempt to answer this question. Peter Shor designing a quantum search algorithm that is much faster than any known classical algorithm marked the beginning of a new paradigm. The most relevant aspect is the way we process information. Doing it the quantum way speeds up the process, makes it more efficient and surpasses, in many cases, the limits known from a classical perspective. This course begins with a discussion on information theory and introduces ideas about quantum information processing (QIP). Other topics to be covered include quantum algorithms and their experimental implementations. Students will learn to program the IBM quantum computer as well. Major corporates in IT and many leading institutes have strong research programs in QIP. That vouches for the importance of this science.

Required for: Required course for PSYC Major, PSYC Minor
Description: The Introduction of Psychology course (PSYC201) introduces students to basic concepts of General Psychology, including topics on perception, learning, memory, intelligence, motivation, emotion, and personality. In this way, it levels the field for students from varied educational settings in school who may have a differentiated exposure to psychology as an academic discipline, and prepares them for an undergraduate training in the field. Going further, the course facilitates and demands a critical examination of the psychological knowledge for real-life problems. PSYC201 is designed to introduce students to some of the classic psychological studies and thereby demonstrate the principles of some of the key areas of modern psychology as a diverse and interdisciplinary science. This course seeks to familiarise the students with the broader questions within the field of psychology and the wide range of theoretical and methodological responses that emerge from psychological knowledge.

This course will introduce the concepts of objectivity and subjectivity, as the mirror conundrums of the discipline of psychology. Psychology is a science that explores and interrogates the psychological basis of being human, from behaviour to neurocognition, from consciousness to the unconscious, from the normal to the pathological, and from the individual to the social. This course will follow the history of ideas in the development of the field, especially at the paradigmatic moments that helped define contemporary psychology. It will introduce students to the scientific method in psychology with its emphasis on objectivity and knowledge generation through empirical research in domains such as behavioural psychology and cognitive psychology. It will then track the different routes to knowledge in psychology in domains such as social psychology and qualitative psychology. The course will explore work emerging from the Global South, drawing on domains of cultural psychology and decolonising psychological science. The final module in this course will take up a contemporary issue besetting psychology today.

Programming for Psychologists is an undergraduate course designed to equip psychology students with computational problem-solving skills. Through hands-on exercises in Python and Octave, students will learn to think like programmers, developing scripts to analyze behavioral data, run simulations, and automate research workflows. Emphasis on real-world applications includes data visualization, statistical modeling, and research practices. The course also introduces LaTeX for creating professional reports and slides for effective presentations. By integrating coding fundamentals with psychological research methods, students will gain practical expertise in computational tools essential for advanced research, enhancing their ability to design experiments, manage datasets, and communicate findings efficiently.

Required for: Required course for PSYC Major, PSYC Minor
Description: This course examines the biological basis of behaviour, and develops an understanding of the complexities of the brain and the mechanisms underlying various behavioural phenomena. How is our brain organised? How do neurons function? What is the brain basis of psychological phenomena? How do our genes and hormones influence behaviour? We will be exploring answers to these questions through interactive lectures. This course introduces various brain disorders as a clinical method to better comprehend the complexity of mind-brain connection. Lastly, we will discuss various brain recording techniques and how they are important to unravel the mystery of the brain. By integrating knowledge from biology and psychology, students gain a holistic understanding of how biological processes shape human behaviour and cognition. This course is designed to provide an introduction to the major concepts, theories, and methods in the field of behavioural neuroscience.

Are you interested to understand the mind and its operations? Do you want to know
more about why intelligence is embodied and know more about the brain, body, and the mind? How are intelligence and cognition; experience and knowledge, thought and consciousness related? These questions can lead us to the most fertile approach to understand the nature of brain, body & the mind. By embracing the fields of Philosophy, Cognitive Psychology, Artificial Intelligence, Neuroscience, Linguistics, Anthropology and Social Cognition the concept embodiment will be conceptualized. In addition, theoretical insights and experimental convergence using multiple methods especially psychological and neurological experiments and computational models will be deliberated to understand the central concepts of embodiment.

This course provides an in-depth exploration of Evolutionary Psychology, an approach that seeks to understand the human mind and behavior through the lens of evolution and natural selection. Rooted in Darwinian theory, evolutionary psychology posits that psychological traits—like physical traits—are adaptations shaped by ancestral environments. This course will examine how evolutionary theory informs our understanding of cognition, emotion, and social behavior, and it will critically assess the evidence and arguments for these claims.
 
Students will trace the historical development of evolutionary psychology, beginning with foundational work in ethology and sociobiology, and leading to contemporary applications in cognitive and social psychology. Topics covered will include mating strategies, kin selection, parental investment, cooperation and conflict, status hierarchies, and moral emotions. Special emphasis will be placed on the interplay between evolved predispositions and cultural variability, highlighting the complex interdependence between biology and environment.
 
Students will engage with both theoretical models and empirical studies, learning to critically evaluate the methodological challenges of testing evolutionary hypotheses. They will also reflect on the ethical and philosophical implications of evolutionary explanations for human behavior. By the end of the course, students will be equipped with a framework for understanding psychological mechanisms as adaptive solutions to recurrent problems in human ancestral environments, while also remaining sensitive to the scientific and societal debates surrounding this approach.

Description: The course examines developmental changes across different domains of development from conception to old age by addressing four fundamental questions related to human development: continuity, plasticity, sources of development, individual differences across cultures. From empirical evidence and theoretical perspectives, students will gain a deeper understanding of how biological predispositions and environmental contexts interact to mold individuals' developmental trajectories across time periods. Students will examine various cognitive processes, including perception, attention, learning, memory, language, problem-solving, reasoning, and thinking. Course Title: Early Childhood Development: interventions, policies and programs
Description:
This course explores the foundational principles of early childhood development (ECD) and the role of interventions and policies in shaping developmental outcomes. Drawing from psychology, public health, education, and social policy, students will examine how early experiences—from birth through age eight—impact cognitive, social-emotional, and physical development.
Through a multidisciplinary lens, the course will critically analyze evidence-based interventions and policy frameworks designed to support children and families, especially in contexts of adversity. Topics include responsive caregiving, early learning, nutrition, health, and child protection, with a focus on global and local examples. Students will engage with case studies, research articles, and policy documents to understand how science translates into practice and how cultural, economic, and institutional factors influence the effectiveness of early childhood programs.
By the end of the course, students will be equipped to evaluate and discuss the design, implementation, and impact of early childhood interventions and policies, and to consider their implications for equity, social justice, and long-term societal well-being.

What does freedom mean? How does it go beyond the lay definition that it lies in the ability to act and speak without constraint? What are the implications of parsing this concept at the individual level or examining it in a relational or collective way? Philosophically, the concept of freedom plays out in the domain of metaphysics and ethics, with theories ranging from the libertarian, the compatibilist, and the deterministic. These transcendental ideas have had a subtle but definite impact on our constitutional guarantees for free speech on the one hand, and the restrictions placed on them on others. What implications does the information we have about inner processes have for the issue of agency? What are the grounds, if any, for coercing opinion and behaviour through pressure? What is the space for freedom of religion in a secular state? What is the distinction between positive and negative liberty and how are these related to notions of libertarianism, collectivism, autonomy and free will? Finally, where is freedom situated in discussions on fairness and justice and what are alternative notions of freedom, for example, as a form of self-realisation or as a model for non-domination. This inter-disciplinary course touches on philosophy, constitutional law, political theory, ethics, jurisprudence and media law.

Description:
This course is an introduction to the basic notions of Fourier analysis. Three classical topics will be explored: Fourier series, Fourier transforms and the discrete Fourier transform. The basic notions, tools and techniques of Fourier analysis are very important in both pure and applied mathematics (in areas such as signal, image and data processing, etc;) and in physics and computer science. This course is designed to be a gentle, concrete introduction to the subject, with a focus on basic examples and with an eye towards applications. 
Prerequisites include the basic notions of linear algebra (matrices, vector spaces and linear independence, linear transformations, eigenvalues and vectors and inner product spaces) and single and multivariable calculus.
It is hoped that this course will be accessible to 3rd year and 4th year students in mathematics, physics, computer science, and data science.

Course Title: Self, State and Society: Philosophical Perspectives
Description: There is an intricate dialectical relation between the concepts of self, state and society, and these relations are negotiated in every age, differently. It is important to understand these relations, as they provide us with the rationale for our understanding of ourselves, and our place in the social and political domains. These relations also determine the possibilities and limits of our own agency and actions vis-à-vis others. This course will introduce some of the fundamental philosophical presuppositions that allow this negotiation to take place in the modern age. The course is divided into three modules that discuss the constitution of the self, the state, and the social, in the contemporary modern western age. The objective of this discussion is to not only present a philosophical analysis of these concepts but to also open them up for critique and alternative readings, either from the classical tradition or in some cases contemporary perspectives. The course is not intended to be comprehensive in its approach to the readings presented, but rather the focus is to have an in-depth engagement with the philosophical presuppositions of the perspectives presented. Some of the fundamental issues taken up would be: How is the notion of the self, constituted and what relation does it bear to the understanding of the modern age, and the state? What are the fundamental presuppositions that characterise the foundations of the modern state? What are some of the theoretical alternatives to this understanding of the state? What is the role of the social, as presented through the institution of the family, in this matrix? What is the relation that the family bears to the state, and the self?

Religion and Society in South Asia
Description:
This course is about the study of Religion with a particular focus on South Asian religions (Hinduism, Jainism, Buddhism, Zorastrianism, Christianity, Islam, and Sikhism), as they have been studied anthropologically, historically and politically – as daily beliefs and practices, and in relation to wider South Asian culture, history and politics. This course will provide both a grounded study of religious practices and religions in Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan, Sikkim, Sri Lanka as well as a postcolonial critique of the study of religions and nationalism in the South Asian realm.
 The course will explore why the transformation of the public sphere in South Asia shows the increasing importance of religious movements, and of the political use of religious symbolism in new communication technologies. One of the most important trends in the present era is the attempt to create a homogenous religious community, not only within the national territorial space, but also in a transnational space. If such attempts offer a sense of identity for communities, it also offers a brutal confrontation with “the Other,” however defined. The violent conflicts between Hindus and Muslims, between “high” castes and Dalits, between Shi’as and Sunnis, between Buddhists and Hindus, Buddhists and Muslims are sad reminders of a growing confrontation which is not only regional, but increasingly global.
